title: Edge-AI Based Distributed Fleet Coordination for Autonomous Mobile Robots (AMRs) in Smart Warehouses
description:
• Background Modern smart warehouses rely on fleets of Autonomous Mobile Robots (AMRs) to move goods efficiently. As fleet sizes grow, relying entirely on a centralized cloud server for path planning causes high network latency, Wi-Fi dead-zone vulnerabilities, and single-point-of-failure risks.To ensure continuous operation, modern robotics is shifting toward decentralized, edge-computing solutions where robots can talk to each other directly and make split-second decisions on the fly.
• Description The objective is to design a decentralized coordination and collision-avoidance framework for a multi-robot fleet (at least 3 AMRs) operating in a dynamic warehouse environment. The system must run locally on edge hardware (e.g., Raspberry Pi or Jetson Nano onboard each robot) and handle:
1. Decentralized Communication: Inter-robot messaging to share position and intent without a central server.
2. Dynamic Multi-Agent Conflict Resolution: Resolving deadlocks and avoiding collisions at narrow intersections or choke points in real-time.
3. Task Allocation & Re-routing: Automatically re-assigning pickup points or changing paths if one robot encounters a blocked aisle.
• Expected Solution A multi-robot simulation featuring:
• Decentralized Network Stack: A peer-to-peer communication protocol where robots share localization data locally.
• Multi-Agent Path Planning: Implementation of algorithms for edge hardware.
• Fleet Dashboard: A lightweight monitoring UI that visualizes the entire fleet's real-time positions and battery status.
• Success Criteria: Zero inter-robot collisions and a minimum 20% reduction in total task completion time compared to traditional stop-and-wait methods when handling overlapping paths.
summary: Innovation (5/5): draws on ai, autonomous, robotics applied to a robotics and drones problem, placing it in the breakthrough band. Feasibility (3/5): as a software build with moderate integration complexity, a full build is tight for 36 hours and will need scope-cutting. Impact (2/5): addresses a more targeted user group within Robotics and Drones. Tech Depth (4/5): centers on real-time, protocol. Sustainability (3/5): will need a maintenance/upkeep plan post-hackathon. Scalability (3/5): currently scoped narrowly and would need rework to scale. Total 20/30 -> Yellow verdict.

detail.title: Edge-AI Based Distributed Fleet Coordination for Autonomous Mobile Robots in Smart Warehouses

overview.in_plain_terms: Build a system where warehouse robots talk directly to each other and make split-second decisions themselves, avoiding collisions and re-routing around blocked paths, instead of depending on a central server that becomes a bottleneck and single point of failure as the fleet grows.
overview.why_it_matters: A centralized coordination system creates real risk, network lag, Wi-Fi dead zones, single point of failure. Genuine peer-to-peer robot coordination removes that dependency entirely.
pain_points: Centralized cloud coordination causes high latency, Wi-Fi dead-zone vulnerability, and single-point-of-failure risk at scale.
No established framework for robots to coordinate directly without a central server.
Dynamic conflict resolution (deadlocks, collisions) at real-time speed is genuinely hard without central oversight.
overview.background: As AMR fleet sizes grow, centralized cloud coordination creates latency and reliability risks, motivating a shift to decentralized, edge-computing coordination where robots communicate and decide directly.
overview.whats_being_asked: A decentralized coordination and collision-avoidance framework for a multi-robot fleet (at least 3 AMRs), running on edge hardware (Raspberry Pi/Jetson Nano), handling decentralized communication, conflict resolution, and dynamic task allocation.
expected_solution: Decentralized inter-robot communication (no central server dependency).
Real-time collision avoidance and deadlock resolution at intersections/choke points.
Dynamic task re-allocation when a robot encounters a blocked path.
Genuine edge deployment on real embedded hardware (Raspberry Pi/Jetson Nano).

analysis.innovation_scope_note: Breakthrough. Genuine decentralized multi-robot coordination without a central authority is active robotics/distributed-systems research territory, a real, hard problem.
analysis.invention_effort_note: High. Requires real distributed-systems protocol design, multi-agent conflict resolution algorithms, and genuine embedded/edge deployment together, substantial technical breadth.

competitive_landscape.note: Requires real robotics hardware (multiple AMRs or robot platforms) and distributed-systems expertise together, a narrow, resource-intensive field.

innovation.note: Genuine decentralized multi-agent coordination without central authority is real, valuable distributed-robotics research territory.

invention.note: Distributed communication protocol, conflict resolution algorithms, and real embedded deployment together represent substantial technical depth.

technical_feasibility.note: Genuine physical AMR fleet (at least 3 real robots) with real edge hardware is a significant resourcing requirement most hackathon teams won't have.

impact_and_benefits.note: Directly improves warehouse automation reliability and scalability, genuine industrial value.

architecture.note: Decentralized communication, conflict-resolution logic, and re-routing across multiple independent agents, genuinely complex distributed architecture.

overall_verdict.reasoning: Yellow, genuinely valuable but requires real physical robot hardware (3+ AMRs) that most hackathon teams won't have access to. Scope to a software simulation of the decentralized coordination logic (multiple simulated robot agents) if physical hardware isn't available, rather than claiming real edge-hardware deployment without it.

evaluator_lens.biggest_strength: Very well-specified technical requirements (decentralized communication, conflict resolution, dynamic re-routing) give a clear, concrete, testable target even in simulation.
evaluator_lens.biggest_risk: Genuine physical multi-robot hardware (at least 3 real AMRs with edge computing) is a significant resourcing barrier, most teams should honestly scope to simulation.
evaluator_lens.validate_before_commit: Confirm whether your team has genuine access to 3+ physical robot platforms with edge computing hardware, if not, scope explicitly to a software simulation demonstrating the decentralized coordination algorithm, clearly labeled as simulated.

idea_0_4: Confirm physical robot hardware access honestly, if unavailable, commit to a software simulation of multiple robot agents.
Design your decentralized communication protocol (peer-to-peer messaging simulating inter-robot coordination).
Split: one person on the communication/coordination protocol, one on the conflict-resolution algorithm.
prototype_4_22: Build your decentralized communication layer (real if hardware available, simulated multi-agent otherwise).
Build your conflict-resolution algorithm for collision avoidance and deadlock breaking at simulated choke points.
Start dynamic task re-allocation logic for blocked-path scenarios.
integration_22_30: Test your system with at least 3 agents (real or simulated) in a scenario designed to create genuine conflicts (narrow intersection, blocked path).
Confirm the system resolves conflicts without central coordination, verify no single point of failure exists in your architecture.
Test task re-allocation when one agent's path is blocked.
polish_30_36: Build a clear visualization showing multiple robots (real or simulated) coordinating and resolving conflicts live.
Rehearse a live demo triggering a deadlock/collision scenario and showing decentralized resolution.
Prepare to be honest about real hardware versus simulation scope.
build_plan.how_to_stand_out: Trigger a genuine conflict scenario live (two agents approaching the same narrow intersection simultaneously) and show them resolve it through peer-to-peer negotiation without any central coordinator involved, that live demonstration of genuinely decentralized decision-making is the actual proof this PS asks for.

strengths: Very well-specified technical requirements give a clear, testable target even in simulation.
Genuine, valuable industrial application if physical hardware is available.
weaknesses: Real physical multi-robot hardware is a significant resourcing barrier for most hackathon teams.
Genuine decentralized distributed-systems design is real, hard engineering, easy to fake with a hidden central coordinator.

team_fit.ideal_ratio: Robotics/distributed-systems-heavy, confirm hardware access early since it fundamentally shapes your approach.
team_fit.approach: Honestly assess hardware access first, this determines real deployment versus simulation scope.

ai_buildability_split.ai_can_build_fast: Standard multi-agent simulation scaffolding and basic message-passing infrastructure.
ai_buildability_split.needs_human_judgment: Designing a genuinely decentralized coordination protocol (no hidden central coordinator) and real conflict-resolution algorithms, that's real distributed-systems engineering judgment.
ai_buildability_split.risk_of_leaning_on_ai_only: A system that claims to be decentralized but actually routes decisions through a hidden central point would misrepresent the core architectural claim this PS is specifically testing for.

data_resource_availability.status: No dataset dependency, resourcing constraint is physical robot hardware access, not data.
data_resource_availability.backup_plan: If physical hardware isn't available, build a genuine multi-agent software simulation, clearly labeled as simulated, demonstrating the same decentralized coordination logic that would run on real edge hardware.

judge_qna.question: Is this running on real physical robots with edge hardware, or simulated?
judge_qna.strong_answer: Be direct about your actual scope, if simulated due to hardware access constraints, explain that clearly and confirm your coordination logic is architected the same way it would run on real edge devices.
judge_qna.follow_up: What would change functionally when deploying this on real Raspberry Pi/Jetson Nano hardware?

judge_qna.question: How do you know this is genuinely decentralized, and not secretly relying on a hidden central coordinator?
judge_qna.strong_answer: Walk through your communication architecture explicitly, showing that no single node holds authoritative state or makes decisions for others, each agent negotiates and decides based on peer-shared information alone.
judge_qna.follow_up: What happens if one agent in your system fails or goes offline, does the rest of the fleet continue functioning?
